Mount Kilimanjaro is Africa's highest peak at nineteen thousand three hundred forty-one feet, located in Tanzania near the Kenyan border. A dormant volcano, it last erupted roughly three hundred sixty thousand years ago and comprises three volcanic cones: Kibo, the highest; Mawenzi; and Shira. Perpetual snows and glaciers cover the crater rim, though these glaciers have shrunk dramatically over the last century due to climate change. Despite its modest elevation compared to Himalayan giants, Kilimanjaro is one of the world's most climbed mountains, cited for the striking contrast between snow-capped summit and equatorial savanna. Climbs typically take five to nine days via multiple routes including Marangu and Machame. No technical climbing is required, making it accessible to non-mountaineers. Altitude acclimatization is the primary challenge, and many climbers experience acute mountain sickness despite the simplicity of the route. The stark contrast between lush rainforest at lower elevations and barren, ice-draped summit exemplifies Kilimanjaro's ecological diversity. Hans Meyer and Ludwig Purtscheller made the first European summit in eighteen eighty-nine, though local populations had likely reached the summit much earlier.
